profiles.name: Roger Ludwig
profiles.description: Roger Ludwig was a poet and musician engaged in work with the poor in Washington, DC. He was a two-time Plowshares activist, participating in Plowshares Number Four (1982) and Trident II Pruning Hooks (1985).
profiles.finding: Congressional Record confirms Plowshares context; no captioned portrait located. Obituary namesakes not independently matched.

profiles.name: Sheila Parks
profiles.description: Sheila Parks was a former college teacher based in Medford, Massachusetts at the time of Trident II Pruning Hooks. No further sourceable biographical detail was found.
profiles.finding: Sheila Ruth Parks Brookline 2025 obituary is a lead requiring continuity with Medford Trident II activist; Texas Sheila Ann Parks rejected as unconfirmed namesake.

profiles.name: Suzanne Schmidt
profiles.description: Suzanne Schmidt was a mother, grandmother, and worker with people with disabilities who lived in the Jonah House resistance community in Baltimore at the time of the Trident II Pruning Hooks action.
profiles.finding: Spokane politician, actress and glass artist results lack Jonah House continuity; no verified portrait.

profiles.name: Luis Rosado
profiles.description: New York-based MLN activist and brother of Julio and Andrés Rosado, jailed for civil contempt for refusing to testify before a federal grand jury investigating the FALN. The Rosado brothers' joint resistance became emblematic of the Puerto Rican independence movement's non-collaboration stance. Documented in PFOC Breakthrough magazine.
profiles.finding: FBI wanted armed-robbery namesake not matched to MLN grand-jury resister; FALN archive context only.

profiles.name: Dorie Clay
profiles.description: Dorie Clay, also reported as Dori or Dorrie Clay, was a New York 8+ grand-jury resister and the spouse of defendant Omowale Clay. She was imprisoned for refusing to testify in the investigation and was released after about three and a half months in 1985.
profiles.query: "Dorie Clay" New York grand jury photo
profiles.finding: D12M anniversary and 603 F.Supp.197 identify grand-jury context; no individually captioned image yet.

profiles.name: Wanda Wareham
profiles.description: Wanda Wareham was a New York 8+ grand-jury resister and the spouse of defendant Roger Wareham. She was confined for refusing to testify in March 1985 and released in June when the grand jury term expired. Contemporary reporting says she was subpoenaed again after release; it does not establish another imprisonment.
profiles.query: "Wanda Wareham" New York grand jury photo
profiles.finding: D12M/court evidence confirms resister context; no individually verified portrait yet.

profiles.name: Stacey Lynn Merkt
profiles.description: Stacey Lynn Merkt was a Methodist lay worker at Casa Óscar Romero, a refugee shelter in San Benito, Texas. She was arrested on February 17, 1984 while helping two Salvadoran adults and a child travel around a Border Patrol checkpoint. A jury convicted her on May 14, and on June 27 the court imposed a 90-day custodial sentence but suspended it in favor of two years’ probation. A second prosecution ended in a February 21, 1985 conspiracy conviction and a 179-day prison sentence. Merkt entered the Federal Correctional Institution in Fort Worth on January 29, 1987. Pregnancy complications led the court to release her on April 17 and convert the remaining 83 days to house arrest.
profiles.finding: Christic archive Guardian May 23 1984 scan captions subject at center; image extraction, resolution, crop and rights need review. Sojourners 1987 additional lead.

profiles.name: María del Socorro Pardo Viuda de Aguilar
profiles.description: Aguilar was a Catholic laywoman and widow ("viuda") from Nogales, Sonora, who sheltered Central American refugees in her home as part of Father Quiñones's parish network. She was the named lead defendant solely because her surname came first alphabetically in the indictment caption — hence the case name U.S. v. Aguilar. She voluntarily entered the U.S. in February 1985 to face charges. During the trial she became a symbol of lay Catholic devotion to the movement, famously placing a rose in the crown of thorns on a Christ figure outside the courthouse before entering for the verdict.
profiles.query: "María del Socorro Pardo Viuda de Aguilar" Sanctuary photo
profiles.finding: Sanctuary court 883 F.2d662 confirms identity; no verified individual portrait.

profiles.name: Martin Holladay
profiles.description: Martin Holladay was a carpenter from Sheffield, Vermont, and the son of three-time Plowshares activist Jean Holladay. Acting alone on Feb. 19, 1985 he entered a Minuteman II missile silo at Whiteman AFB near Odessa, Missouri, damaged the silo lid and electrical boxes with hammer and chisel, poured blood, and spray-painted "No More Hiroshimas." When the alarm-response team arrived with automatic rifles he assured them, "Don't worry, I'm unarmed." He later became a well-known building-science writer.
profiles.finding: Washington Post 1986 and court 797 F.2d580 confirm activist. Later building-science author continuity and institutional portrait pending. Military flight-suit namesake not matched.

profiles.name: Jean G. Ford
profiles.description: Jean G. Ford is a Haitian-born physician who graduated from Columbia University’s medical school in May 1984 and trained in internal medicine at Harlem Hospital. He organized against apartheid and police brutality through the Sunrise Collective and the Mobilization Committee Against Police Brutality. Ford was confined at the Metropolitan Correctional Center from January 28 to July 26, 1985 after refusing to testify before the grand jury investigating the New York 8+, citing spousal privilege and his opposition to political intelligence gathering. He later directed the Harlem Lung Center and held senior academic and hospital leadership posts.
profiles.finding: Physician biography/about.me and ResearchGate lead plausibly match Haitian physician; stronger institutional image attribution and continuity pending.

profiles.name: Michelle Thomas
profiles.description: Michelle Thomas was a Rutgers medical student and political activist involved with the Sunrise Collective. She was confined at the Metropolitan Correctional Center for refusing to testify before the grand jury investigating the New York 8+. Her incarceration interrupted her medical studies. The court ordered her release after finding that further detention would not make her testify.
profiles.finding: Rutgers medical-student identity supported by Freedom Archives June1985; actress/counselor/artist namesakes rejected.

profiles.name: Olive Armstrong
profiles.description: Olive Armstrong was one of the New York 8+ grand-jury resisters jailed for refusing to testify in the investigation of Black political activists. Contemporary reporting and a federal court opinion establish confinement over several months in 1985 and her release that July.
profiles.finding: Republic of New Afrika list and Militant4937 corroborate context; no portrait established.

profiles.name: Milton Parish
profiles.description: Milton Parish, also reported as Milton Parrish, was a writer jailed for refusing grand-jury testimony in the New York 8+ investigation. In granting his release, the court concluded that further confinement would reinforce rather than overcome his solidarity with people associated with the Sunrise Collective.
profiles.finding: Alias Milton Parrish confirmed by court and Militant4929. UK Milton parish image archive unrelated. No individual portrait.

profiles.name: Jacqueline Bernard
profiles.description: Jacqueline Bernard, also reported as Jackie Bernard, was a New York 8+ grand-jury resister. She spent months in federal custody in 1985 after refusing to testify in the investigation of Black political activists. Contemporary reporting and a later federal court opinion document her confinement and release.
profiles.finding: Jackie Bernard alias in Freedom Archives June1985; Cameroon Flickr namesake not matched.

profiles.name: James A. Corbett
profiles.description: James A. “Jim” Corbett was a Quaker rancher, philosopher, writer, and co-founder of the Sanctuary Movement. Born in Casper, Wyoming, on October 8, 1933, he began assisting Salvadoran refugees in 1981 and worked with the Rev. John Fife to make Southside Presbyterian Church a public sanctuary in March 1982. A federal indictment in January 1985 charged Corbett and ten others with helping Central American refugees enter and travel through the United States. A jury acquitted him of every charge on May 1, 1986. He died at his Cascabel, Arizona ranch on August 2, 2001.
profiles.finding: Jim Corbett Sanctuary alias yields Quaker Theology, Friends Journal and Weber University essays; recognizable image and creator verification pending. Hunter-naturalist namesake rejected.

profiles.name: Lateefah Carter
profiles.description: Black liberation activist charged as a New York 8+ defendant in the October 17-18, 1984 federal RICO indictment alleging a conspiracy to free Sundiata Acoli, commit armed bank expropriations, and bomb federal buildings. Arrested in a predawn FBI/NYPD Joint Terrorism Task Force raid and held without bail in federal custody before being released pending trial in early 1985. Trial began May 13, 1985 before Judge Kevin Thomas Duffy in the Southern District of New York; the August 1985 jury acquitted her of all RICO and conspiracy counts.
profiles.finding: D12M NY8 anniversary group captions front-row-left subject; clean crop and source rights pending.

profiles.name: Yvette Kelley

Arrested in a predawn FBI/NYPD Joint Terrorism Task Force raid and held without bail in federal custody before being released pending trial in early 1985. Trial began May 13, 1985 before Judge Kevin Thomas Duffy in the Southern District of New York; the August 1985 jury acquitted her of all conspiracy counts.
profiles.finding: D12M group captions Yvette Kelly front row; verify crop/rights and spelling continuity before use.

profiles.name: Roger Wareham
profiles.description: Civil rights attorney and December 12th Movement co-founder, charged as a New York 8+ defendant in the October 17-18, 1984 federal RICO indictment alleging a Black liberation conspiracy to free Sundiata Acoli, commit armed bank expropriations, and bomb federal buildings. Arrested in a predawn FBI/NYPD Joint Terrorism Task Force raid and held without bail in federal custody before being released pending trial in early 1985. Trial began May 13, 1985 before Judge Kevin Thomas Duffy in the Southern District of New York; the August 1985 jury acquitted him on every count. He continued practicing reparations law and pan-African human-rights advocacy, serving as legal counsel to the International Association Against Torture and to delegations on the rights of African people before the United Nations Working Group of Experts on People of African Descent.
profiles.finding: D12M group and attorney listing plausible; reject accountant and grants-director namesakes. Individual portrait provenance pending.

profiles.name: Frank Panopoulos
profiles.description: Frank Panopoulos has worked on peace and social justice issues since 1979. During the 1980s he lived in the Cor Jesu Community, a lay Catholic community engaged in works of mercy in Upper Manhattan. He served prison time for two Plowshares actions (AVCO 1983 and Trident II 1984) and later became a human rights attorney and a writer for CovertAction Magazine.

profiles.name: Jim Barr
profiles.description:
Irish republican supporter held at the Philadelphia Detention Center in connection with US federal charges arising from solidarity with the IRA. Documented in PFOC Breakthrough magazine.

James Gerard Barr was a member of the Irish National Liberation Army (INLA) and the Irish Republican Socialist Party (IRSP). Named by a supergrass informer, he fled to the United States, where the U.K. sought his extradition on an attempted-murder charge from Northern Ireland. He was held for some seventeen months at the Philadelphia Detention Center until a U.S. federal court denied the extradition request in 1985 for insufficient evidence — a rare such denial. He was later granted political asylum in the United States in 1993.
profiles.finding: Full alias James Gerard Barr confirmed by OJP1985 report and extradition619 F.Supp1068. Art collector/musician namesakes rejected; no portrait.

profiles.name: Carlos Noya Muratti
profiles.description: Carlos Noya Muratti was a carpenter, Puerto Rican independence activist, and member of the political bureau of the Liga Socialista Puertorriqueña. He also represented the Liga in the Comité Unitario Contra la Represión. A federal court jailed him for civil contempt on October 30, 1980, after he refused to answer questions or provide evidence to a grand jury investigating the independence movement. He was transferred to the Metropolitan Correctional Center in New York and released on March 27, 1982, after 17 months. Noya again refused to testify before a Brooklyn grand jury in 1983. After an initial mistrial and a second criminal-contempt trial, he received a two-year sentence on April 9, 1984 and was released in December 1985. He continued organizing for political prisoners and Puerto Rican independence until his death in May 2005.
profiles.finding: Juan Mari Bras Vol42 and LibertadNov1985 confirm Federico/Carlos context; no verified portrait extracted.

profiles.name: Jack Elder
profiles.description: Catholic layman who directed Casa Oscar Romero in San Benito, Texas (Diocese of Brownsville) from 1983 — a refugee shelter for Salvadorans and Guatemalans fleeing the U.S.-backed wars. The most prominent Sanctuary Movement defendant prosecuted outside the Tucson trial. Federally indicted 1984. Convicted February 21, 1985 with co-worker Stacey Lynn Merkt of conspiracy and transporting/bringing in undocumented refugees (six counts). Initially sentenced to two years probation but rejected the gag order forbidding sanctuary work or public discussion; resentenced to 150 days in a San Antonio halfway house. Judge Filemón Vela Sr. noted on the record that he "agree[d] with the ends of the sanctuary movement." Co-founded RAICES with Stacey Merkt after release.
profiles.finding: Echoes2017 Old School Activism and VVAW memorial have matching Sanctuary biography/photos; inspect image asset/credit and rights next. Notre Dame football namesake rejected.

profiles.name: Mary Dianne Muhlenkamp
profiles.description: Catholic religious sister from Indiana volunteering with the Diocese of Brownsville, Texas. Arrested by the U.S. Border Patrol on February 17, 1984 near Guerra, Texas while transporting Salvadoran refugees in a diocesan vehicle (Stacey Lynn Merkt was a passenger and was charged separately). A co-defendant in early Sanctuary Movement Texas prosecutions, but the federal government dropped the principal smuggling charge in exchange for her testimony, granting her a one-year deferred adjudication. Her case is significant as one of the first Sanctuary-related arrests of a Catholic sister and helped catalyze the Tucson and Brownsville prosecutions that followed.
profiles.finding: Dianne Muhlenkamp alias confirmed by UPI1985 and Reagan Library sanctuary file. No verified individual portrait yet.

profiles.name: Sondra Clark
profiles.description: Sondra Clark was a Black resident of Battle Creek, Michigan, caught up in the 1984 Calhoun County state grand jury that subpoenaed as many as 200 people from the Black community — children among them — in a campaign against the Coalition to End Police Brutality and Racism and its leader Larry Guy. Clark refused to collaborate and was jailed for contempt even though she was still breast-feeding her seven-month-old child. The child died during her jailing; the movement press reported that the judge had ignored the pleas of her doctors in ordering her held. Reconstructed from the John Brown Anti-Klan Committee newspaper Stop the Grand Jury! (November 1984); further case details have not been located.
profiles.query: "Sondra Clark" Battle Creek grand jury photo
profiles.finding: Exact-name and Battle Creek/grand-jury followups did not establish a usable portrait; retain missing-photo treatment.

profiles.name: Herwig Jantschik
profiles.description: Herwig Jantschik was a West German peace activist and one of three Germans (with Wolfgang Sternstein and Karin Vix) who joined Carl Kabat in carrying out the first Plowshares action in Europe at the U.S. Army's Pershing II base in Schwäbisch-Gmünd. The four had previously distributed booklets about Plowshares actions during a six-week peace march through Germany.
profiles.finding: ZEIT1985 corroborates Plowshares identity. Aalen/Nepal charity social-worker image requires continuity verification.

profiles.name: Karin Vix
profiles.description: Karin Vix was a West German peace activist who joined Carl Kabat, Wolfgang Sternstein and Herwig Jantschik in the December 1983 Plowshares Number Seven action — the first Plowshares action in Europe — disarming a Pershing II missile launcher at the U.S. Army base in Schwäbisch-Gmünd.
profiles.finding: ZEIT1985 corroborates German Plowshares identity; no individual portrait established.

profiles.name: Karl Smith
profiles.description: Karl Smith was 27 at the time of the Griffiss action and a member of the Jonah House resistance community in Baltimore. He had previously been imprisoned with James Cunningham for 60 days for trespassing at the Trident plant in Bangor, Washington, before they both joined Jonah House.
profiles.finding: Washington Post1981 Jonah House context; JetPhotos photographer not matched.

profiles.name: Vernon Joseph Rossman
profiles.description:
Vern Rossman was an ordained minister of the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ), born Feb. 3, 1927, raised in a minister's family in Oklahoma, educated at Phillips University and Yale Divinity School (ordained 1951). He served as a missionary to Japan from 1952 to 1963, where the legacy of Hiroshima and Nagasaki shaped his lifelong commitment to peace and anti-nuclear work; he later worked for the Disciples' Division of Overseas Ministries in Indianapolis and as executive director of Intermedia in NYC under the World Council of Churches. At the time of Griffiss he was a 56-year-old father and grandfather living in Dorchester, MA. He died at his home in Columbia, Missouri in 2014.

Plowshares peace activist arrested in a disarmament action against nuclear weapons systems in the 1980s. Convicted of federal sabotage and depredation of government property. Documented in PFOC Breakthrough magazine.
profiles.finding: Global Ministries missionary obituary located under Vern Rossman; verify dates/biography and portrait before use. Genealogy namesake dates conflict.

profiles.name: Federico Cintrón-Fiallo
profiles.description:
Puerto Rican independentista jailed on civil contempt charges for refusing to testify before a federal grand jury investigating the clandestine independence movement. His resistance was widely supported by the Puerto Rican left and human rights organizations. Documented in PFOC Breakthrough magazine.

Federico Cintrón Fiallo, a Puerto Rican independence activist and socialist from Arecibo (and brother of Macheteros commander Norberto Cintrón Fiallo), refused — with Carlos Noya — to testify before a federal grand jury in Brooklyn investigating the FALN in 1983, telling the court their refusal stemmed from "a struggle of liberation." After an August 1983 mistrial he was convicted of criminal contempt in October 1983, and on April 9, 1984 U.S. District Judge Eugene Nickerson sentenced him to two years in prison; he was imprisoned until a judge ordered his release in 1985. He is identified as a leader of the Fuerzas Armadas de Resistencia Popular (FARP) and later earned a doctorate and became a university professor.

Executive secretary of Puerto Rico's United Workers Movement (MOU) labor federation, arrested in Aug. 1975 by FBI and undercover agents on bank-robbery charges as he prepared to attend a solidarity conference in Havana; The Black Panther Vol. 14 no.6 (1975) reports his attorneys called it an attempt to cripple organized labor and the independence movement.
profiles.finding: Spanish author/interview and NYU Palante archival sources found; named portrait/rights and activist continuity still require verification.

profiles.name: Erica Bouza
profiles.description: Erica Bouza was the wife of then-Minneapolis Police Chief Tony Bouza. Became national news in April 1983 when she and 138 other anti-nuclear protesters sat down in front of Honeywell's Minneapolis headquarters and were arrested by officers under her husband's command. Arrested again on October 24, 1983 in the second mass sit-in (577 arrests) and sentenced to 10 days at the Hennepin County workhouse. Featured in People Magazine. The first of approximately 11 peace-related civil-disobedience arrests in the Twin Cities.
profiles.finding: Star Tribune2023 obituary explicitly matches Tony Bouza spouse/peace activism and includes1983 photo; MNHS Frank Trnka archive alternate. Asset/credit review pending.

profiles.name: George W. Crocker
profiles.description: One of Minnesota's longest-serving energy and anti-nuclear activists, working since the late 1970s on energy-democracy and anti-nuclear-power issues. A member of the Northern Sun Alliance (the Minnesota anti-nuclear coalition), a frequent collaborator with Marv Davidov at the Honeywell Project, and longtime executive director of the North American Water Office. Author of "About Power: How to Democratize Electricity Now."
profiles.finding: NAWO official staff/history confirms George Crocker role; no individual portrait established.

profiles.name: Jamie Bauer

profiles.name: Mary Lyons

profiles.name: Roberto Caldero
profiles.description: Chicago Puerto Rican community organizer and MLN activist jailed for civil contempt after refusing to testify before a federal grand jury investigating the FALN. His resistance was part of a broad campaign of non-collaboration by independentistas in the early 1980s. Documented in PFOC Breakthrough magazine.

profiles.name: José López
profiles.description: Chicago-based leader of the Movimiento de Liberación Nacional Puertorriqueño (MLN) and longtime director of the Puerto Rican Cultural Center in Humboldt Park; brother of Oscar López Rivera. Jailed for civil contempt for refusing to cooperate with federal grand juries investigating the FALN in the late 1970s and 1980s. Documented in PFOC Breakthrough magazine.
profiles.query: "José López" Puerto Rican Cultural Center photo
profiles.finding: PRCC2016 No Ones an Island, NMPRAC board, PBS and La Voz strong institutional leads; asset and source-credit verification pending.

profiles.name: José Luis Rodríguez
profiles.description: José Luis Rodríguez was one of four people arrested in the Chicago area on June 29, 1983 in a major FALN case after months of FBI surveillance, in which the government alleged a plot targeting military installations. After a 1985 trial he was convicted of one count of seditious conspiracy (18 U.S.C. § 2384) but — unlike co-defendants Alberto Rodríguez, Edwin Cortés, and Alejandrina Torres, who received 35-year terms — was given a suspended sentence and five years' probation; his conviction was affirmed by the Seventh Circuit in 1986 (United States v. Rodriguez, 803 F.2d 318). At trial he affirmed support for Puerto Rican independence while denying FALN membership. (This identification is based on the Chicago FALN seditious-conspiracy case; the very common name makes certainty difficult.)
profiles.finding: Washington Post1983, GovInfo and AP1985 distinguish student from Alberto Rodriguez. No verified portrait; do not substitute co-defendant.

profiles.name: Daniel Rutt
profiles.description: Christian pacifist of Mennonite family background raised Methodist. Prosecuted after publicly writing officials and giving a local newspaper interview saying he would never register. Sentenced to a few months at a federal detention facility in the Detroit area, with work release allowing him to drive 70 miles daily to his job. Later careers in public health and design.
profiles.finding: Dan Rutt alias confirmed by Fifth Estate1986 and Workers Advocate1983; protest group photo lacks individual identification.

profiles.name: Patricia McCormick
profiles.description: Sister of Loretto raised on a farm northwest of Chicago, served in Bolivia in 1965 where she met Daniel Berrigan during her formation in Cuernavaca. After returning to Denver she trained at the Ground Zero Center for Nonviolent Action and formed an interfaith group vigiling at Rocky Flats' west gate. In April 1983 she and a Mennonite friend entered the Rocky Flats plant and poured a vial of blood on a facility sign; she was charged with a misdemeanor and served two months in jail.
profiles.finding: Verified caption and matching Rocky Flats1983 account in NCR July8 2017 interview. Original770x1033 JPEG deployed; publisher credit preserved and no open license claimed. Data discrepancy flagged for separate review: NCR reports age81 in2017, while site DOB is1942; biography/action evidence establishes identity. DOB was not changed.

profiles.name: Karol Schulkin
profiles.description: Early Ground Zero member arrested with Shelley Douglass and Mary Grondin walking the warhead rail line into Bangor naval base on Ash Wednesday, Feb 16, 1983. Told the court: "I must stand up and say, no more — no more bombings and burning of people and lands."
profiles.finding: ArchivesWest Ground Zero visual collection and Sojourners1984 lead; individual image identification and rights pending.

profiles.name: Mary Grondin
profiles.description: Ground Zero Center member who walked the Trident rail line at Bangor with Shelley Douglass and Karol Schulkin on Ash Wednesday, Feb 16, 1983, posting atomic-bomb-victim photographs along the way before being arrested.
profiles.finding: ArchivesWest Ground Zero visual collection and Street Spirit2015 lead; individual image identification pending. Texas2026 obituary/genealogy namesakes not matched.

profiles.name: Alberto de Jesús Berríos
profiles.description: Alberto de Jesús Berríos was a Puerto Rican independence activist — for years a distributor of the Puerto Rican Socialist Party newspaper and an activist in the National Support Committee for Vieques — who became the first name on the FBI list of 25 people and groups drawn up after the December 3, 1979 attack on a U.S. Navy bus at Sabana Seca. Subjected to constant FBI surveillance and harassment though never charged in the attack, he left the island in 1980 and settled in Green Bay, Wisconsin, working as a cabinet maker. On January 17, 1983 he was arrested as a supposed fugitive and brought before the federal grand jury investigating Sabana Seca; when he refused to testify he was jailed nine months for civil contempt, first in New York City and then in Miami. Two days before his contempt term was up, the government charged him with misuse of a social security number — from the false identity he had used to escape the harassment — and set bail at two million dollars, later reduced. He was convicted in January 1984 and was awaiting sentencing when The Militant interviewed him that spring; a De Jesús Support Association organized in Wisconsin around his defense. Reconstructed from The Militant, April 6, 1984; the sentencing outcome has not been located.
profiles.query: "Alberto de Jesús Berríos" grand jury Wisconsin photo
profiles.finding: Militant4812 and court706 F.2d355 corroborate grand-jury case; no verified image. Do not conflate with Tito Kayak.

profiles.name: Larry Morlan
profiles.description:
Larry Morlan was a Catholic peace activist arrested in a Plowshares disarmament action against nuclear weapons systems in the 1980s and held at FCI Sandstone, Minnesota. Convicted of federal sabotage and depredation of government property. Documented in PFOC Breakthrough magazine.

Father Larry Morlan was a Catholic priest of the Diocese of Peoria, Illinois who participated in the Gods of Metal Plowshares action at Andrews Air Force Base Open House in May 1998 - hammering on a B-52 bomber. Sentenced to 4 months in federal prison on January 4, 1999.
profiles.finding: Washington Post1998 and Jean Gump retrospective match Plowshares priest. Group image position unresolved; Barberton obituary and Dellinger photograph not suitable.
